prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which brought atomic frequency standards to unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks have the cleanest combination of originality, attribution and maturity on this shortlist. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the trade-off between trapping and light shifts, and Ye's group turned it into a many-atom clock at the 1e-18 level with demonstrated physics reach: relativistic redshift across millimetres, constraints on varying constants, dark-matter searches, and a credible path to redefining the second. It was independently reproduced and compared across continents, so there is no question of premature recognition. Six of the eight opening ballots rank it, five of them in the top three, which is the broadest support of any candidate, and two of us put it first. I opened with IceCube first and still regard that as a major discovery in nature, but the colleagues' attribution and maturity arguments below move me to put the clocks first. The 2005 prize covered the frequency comb that these clocks use; it did not cover the lattice-clock concept, and the citation should be drawn on that boundary.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is a measurement invention rather than a discovery of a new phenomenon, and the line from ion clocks (partly covered in 2012) and the comb (2005) is arguable, so the committee may see a third prize in precision spectroscopy as incremental. The SI second has not yet been redefined, so one could wait for that moment. A two-name prize also leaves out strong clock groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST, and Ye's record also rests on his comb-based work, which makes the exact scope of his credit a judgement call.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked IceCube first as a genuine new window on the universe with clear conceptual novelty, proposed Halzen and Karle only, and ranked twisted bilayer graphene second and the lattice clock third.
responses.response: I agree on the science and ranked IceCube first myself. Where I now differ is on attribution. You propose two names and note that the split is not settled for you; I make the same cut, but I am an instrumentalist and I know how many people built AMANDA and IceCube. A two-person IceCube prize would leave out the drilling, optical-module and calibration teams whose work made the detector possible, and the source associations are still at modest significance. A clock prize with two clearly identified originators does not carry that cost. I would keep IceCube as the first alternative and revisit it when NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane are corroborated by KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked IceCube fourth and called a three-person credit within a collaboration of hundreds somewhat arbitrary, adding that the physical results are as yet less deep than the instrument; he put fluctuation theorems first, as exact and now extensively tested.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously and it has changed my ranking; I would not call it a reason to dismiss IceCube, since the diffuse flux is established and the question of where cosmic rays are accelerated is deep, but I accept that credit is the weak point. On fluctuation theorems, I respect the exactness and the experimental tests, but I do not see a single decisive experimental or conceptual moment, and you yourself note that priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Gallavotti, Jarzynski and Crooks is contested and that Crooks and Seifert have claims the three-name limit cannot satisfy. By comparison the lattice-clock credit is much cleaner, which is why I put it ahead.

responses.point: Kroll ranked the lattice clock first as the cleanest case of a change in what can be measured, with Katori's concept and Ye's record performance, and asked whether Ye should be credited mainly through the comb or the lattice clock.
responses.response: I agree with your assessment, and your question about Ye is the one I want settled before a final ballot. My view is that the citation should be anchored on the lattice-clock concept and its realisation, so that the comb, already honoured in 2005, is only the enabling technology; Ye's role in bringing the lattice clock to its accuracy and stability, and in the many-body clock work, is then a separate and sufficient basis for credit. Where I would qualify your view slightly is on 'arguably overdue': I would stress that the missing SI redefinition is a reason some colleagues may want to wait, and we should be explicit about why we do not.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked altermagnetism first and dynamical mean-field theory second, and for twisted bilayer graphene noted that the interpretation is not stable enough yet, so recognition may be somewhat early.
responses.response: I share your reservation about twisted bilayer graphene: I ranked it third and I regard the unresolved pairing mechanism and the sample-to-sample variability as a real argument for waiting, even though the prediction followed by decisive experiments is an attractive story. Altermagnetism is a different matter. It has attracted only your first-place vote, with no other member ranking it, and you yourself note unresolved priority relative to earlier symmetry-based work and an unestablished materials picture. That is the opposite of a settled prize case, and I would need to hear a stronger argument on maturity before treating it as a competitor to the clocks.

responses.point: Olsson ranked twisted bilayer graphene first as a clear discovery with a theory-plus-experiment split that supports Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, and ranked the lattice clock second as an invention with a well-identified origin.
responses.response: We agree on the clocks, and I value that you read it as exactly the kind of invention with a well-identified origin that the prize is meant to recognise. On twisted bilayer graphene I accept your attribution case, and it is better than the case for IceCube: the theoretical prediction and the decisive experiment fall to identifiable people. My difference is timing. Eight years is short, the origin of superconductivity is open, and Cao and the other first-author experimentalists are not on the supplied credit. I would keep it as my second alternative, and I would support it more readily in a few years if a pairing mechanism emerges.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat a third precision-spectroscopy or clock prize after 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion control) as sufficiently distinct, and whether it would rather wait for the redefinition of the second.

Exactly how much of Jun Ye's credit rests on the lattice clock itself rather than on the comb and broader clock programme, and whether other lattice-clock proposers or realisers are inadequately represented by the two supplied names.
Whether a two-person prize is better than a combination with a second part; no second part can be added without removing one of the two clock laureates because of the three-person limit.
How much weight the committee should place on recency of the source associations for IceCube, and whether independent confirmation from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD changes the maturity assessment.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile with any of the credited names on the shortlist. I do declare professional proximity to astroparticle physics, since IceCube (B029) is in my own field, and my experience with the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and PoGO collaborations, and I do not claim any documented tie to IceCube or its named individuals; I have tried to apply the same standard to it as to the others, and my preferred configuration is outside my field.
